entries.title: Israeli forces demolish homes in southern Lebanon
entries.summary: Israeli excavators demolished homes in Zawtar al-Sharqiye in southern Lebanon.
entries.content:
Israeli forces demolish homes in southern Lebanon

NewsFeed

Israeli forces demolish homes in southern Lebanon

Israeli excavators demolished homes in Zawtar al-Sharqiye in southern Lebanon, one of the first pilot zones where the Lebanese army deployed under a framework agreement reached with Israel in June. Israel’s occupation has made large parts of the border region uninhabitable.

Published On 18 Nov 2026

entries.title: US official says Hormuz insurance hits $64m: Is the strait really open?
entries.summary: Hung Cao says shipping insurance costs have soared to $64m for a single transit, challenging claims the strait is open.
entries.content:
Hung Cao says insurance costs have soared to $64m for a single transit, challenging Trump’s repeated claims the Strait of Hormuz is open for business.

A senior United States Navy official has claimed that insurance costs for commercial ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz have soared to $64m for a single transit, highlighting the enormous economic toll of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao made the remarks during a Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing on Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the cost of the war and its impact on freedom of navigation.

After the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, Iran in effect closed the strait, allowing only some ships to pass while targeting those it says are unauthorised. This has raised the risks for shipping in the strait exponentially and caused severe shortages of oil, gas, fertiliser and other essential products from Gulf producers usually shipped via this route.

Cao’s claim has not been independently verified and challenges previously reported rises in insurance costs over the course of the nine-month-old conflict.

The remarks come as US President Donald Trump insists that the military campaign against Iran is effectively over, and that the US Navy is successfully escorting ships through the strait, even as new attacks on oil tankers and continued restrictions on shipping raise questions about whether one of the world’s most important energy waterways is really open.

The strait, the only sea route from the Gulf to the Arabian Sea and the open ocean beyond, carried about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the war began.

Although some vessels are still navigating the waterway, shipping remains substantially below pre-war levels, while Iran and the US continue to impose competing restrictions.

Here’s what we know.

What did Hung Cao say in the Senate hearing?

During an exchange with Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, Cao said insurance costs for commercial vessels had risen dramatically since the conflict began.

He initially cited an insurance cost of $54,000 for a single crossing before clarifying that that was what insurance had previously cost, before the war. The cost now, he said, stood at $64m.

Slotkin responded by blaming the war for the increase, arguing that commercial vessels no longer enjoyed the same freedom of navigation they had before the conflict.

Cao also detailed the strain the war has placed on the US Navy, including prolonged deployments, deteriorating conditions and pressure on military resources.

“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” he told lawmakers.

Democrats accused Cao of being a Trump “yes man” on the US-Israeli war on Iran, and downplaying its toll on sailors’ mental health after eight suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York, asked him about a sailor who went overboard.

“Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself and he admitted that,” Cao told her, saying he used ‌a life preserver.

Gillibrand responded: “What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?”

“I think you are minimising what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand replied, while dismissing Cao’s response as “inhumane”.

Did Cao misstate the cost of insurance?

Cao’s $64m figure appears unusually high, even by the standards of wartime shipping insurance.

There is no independently verified evidence that $64m is the current insurance premium for a regular commercial vessel crossing the volatile strait.

“He gave no context. Is he talking about additional premiums for war risk insurance which are set as a percentage of hull value?” Michelle Bockmann, an analyst at maritime intelligence company Windward, told Al Jazeera.

“If so, it depends on the vessel type and the rate paid in order to get proper perspective.”

In July, a report published by S&P Global said that war-risk insurance premiums had climbed to between 7.5 and 10 percent of a ship’s hull value, compared with 1 to 3 percent previously.

It estimated that insurance for a tanker carrying 270,000 metric tonnes of crude could, therefore, cost approximately $21m.

Separately, Reuters news agency reported in September that the cost of moving an oil cargo through Hormuz had risen to roughly $10m-$20m, quoting an executive at Dubai’s Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC).

Why are insurance rates so high?

Regardless of whether it now costs $20m or $60m for insurance to transit the Strait of Hormuz, premiums have surged because ships face the possibility of being struck by missiles, drones or naval mines while passing through the waterway.

War-risk insurance covers vessels against losses arising from military conflict. Its price depends on the value of the vessel, the cargo and the likelihood of an attack.

Higher insurance costs can also feed into freight rates, fuel prices and the cost of goods transported around the world.

Is the Hormuz strait really open?

Technically, yes. But it remains far from fully and freely open as it was before the war.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest weekly report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

The UKMTO recorded 308 vessel crossings during the seven days ending November 11, comprising 139 outbound and 169 inbound journeys.

Nevertheless, Trump has repeatedly suggested that Washington has secured shipping through the strait by providing naval escorts and maintaining the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Meanwhile, Iran insists that it, in fact, controls the passage of shipping through the strait.

Tehran has demanded that vessels use approved routes and coordinate with its forces. It has also announced exemptions for ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar.

The route approved by Iran takes ships much closer to its own coastline than they used to sail, as the map below shows:

The continuing dangers to ships ignoring Iran’s warnings were demonstrated this week.

On Monday, UKMTO reported two tanker attacks, including one near Oman that left a vessel disabled and its engine room on fire. The following day, Iranian forces claimed three additional tankers had struck naval mines.

On Tuesday, the US attacked targets on Iran’s Qeshm island, near Hormuz, following an Iranian drone attack targeting US military installations in Bahrain in recent days.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, said the strait could, therefore, hardly be considered open under normal circumstances.

“It is only open for business if mariners are prepared to take these risks, and it certainly isn’t open by any pre-war definition of the word,” he told Al Jazeera.

“It remains a miracle that we have avoided an energy crisis, and the longer this goes on, the more the alternatives will be developed.”

But Beauchamp said resolving the crisis would require Washington to confront the limits of its influence in the region.

“I can’t see a way that doesn’t involve conceding that the US does not have the ability to order things in the Middle East as it would wish,” he said.

entries.title: Palestinians flee refugee camp as Israel begins operation in central Gaza
entries.summary: Israeli army says the operation west of the 'Yellow Line' aims to 'eliminate a threat'.
entries.content:
Israeli army says the operation west of the ‘Yellow Line’ aims to ‘eliminate a threat’.

Israeli forces have killed three Palestinians during a new operation in central Gaza, according to hospital officials.

Al Jazeera correspondents in Gaza are reporting that Israeli tanks were operating on Wednesday near Salah al-Din Street, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij camp, amid shooting by drones and shelling.

An Israeli air strike targeted the town of al-Mughraqa, north of the Nuseirat camp, killing one person and injuring several others, an official at al-Awda Hospital told Al Jazeera.

Earlier on Wednesday the Israeli army said the operation aimed to “eliminate a threat” to its forces operating in the area of the “Yellow Line”.

The “Yellow Line” demarcates the Israeli-occupied area of Gaza and was established under the October 2025 Gaza “ceasefire”.

In a statement, the Israeli military said: “We reserve the freedom to act and manoeuvre whenever necessary to eliminate any immediate threat in the Gaza Strip.”

Al Jazeera correspondents reported that families fled the northern part of the Nuseirat refugee camp on Wednesday as well as areas near the Israeli military operations.

Deadly attacks

Before the announcement of the Israeli operation, two Israeli drone attacks on the Gaza Strip killed at least two people, hospital officials told Al Jazeera.

Al-Shifa Hospital reported that one person was killed and others were wounded in an attack on the Sheikh Ijlin neighbourhood in southwestern Gaza City.

Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital reported one person was killed in a separate attack on Deir el-Balah in central Gaza, where the hospital had earlier reported an injury.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health said on Wednesday that hospitals recorded seven deaths and received 15 wounded people in the previous 24 hours.

Six people were killed by Israel over that period while one died from injuries caused by an earlier attack, the ministry said.

entries.title: ‘Status quo’ between US and Iran could break out into war, analysts warn
entries.summary: Iran and the US have continued to exchange strikes in recent days, but all-out war has so far been avoided.
entries.content:
Iran and the US have continued to exchange strikes in recent days, but all-out war has so far been avoided.

Tehran, Iran – Iranian forces have targeted military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait as the United States has hit military and radar installations in southern Iran after a spate of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Both the US and Iran appear reluctant for all-out conflict again, as happened during the opening weeks of the war, which the US and Israel began on February 28. But analysts said the current situation is inherently unstable and could potentially escalate again into full-blown war that could see Israel rejoin the strikes on Iran.

US forces are deployed at military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait, which Tehran considers complicit in the recent strikes on southern Iran. The two countries had not been attacked since early September, but both have been targeted by Iranian drones in recent days.

The lull for Bahrain ended on November 13 when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) directed explosive-laden drones towards the Riffa Air Base after US air strikes in Sirik, a port on Iran’s Hormozgan coast. Several more Iranian strikes have followed, and the US has also attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island on multiple occasions.

After hitting Bahrain, the IRGC warned Manama against its security partnership with the US and its treatment of Shia Muslim leaders after several were recently given lengthy prison sentences.

Kuwait reported incoming drones overnight into Wednesday. Iran’s military said it was targeting US equipment at Ali Al Salem Air Base, including missile launch platforms. No Iranian missiles were used against Bahrain or Kuwait, unlike attacks earlier in the war, according to reports.

Mohammad Eslami, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst, said Iran aims to gradually degrade US military assets across the region, particularly those Tehran believes were active during the war.

“So long as the war does not end in a political agreement, Iran will continue to do this, regardless of other factors like the blockade,” he told Al Jazeera.

US President Donald Trump and senior officials in his administration have insisted a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports and tough sanctions against Tehran are working. These appear designed to either force Iran to concede to US demands for ending the war or lead to the collapse of its government.

But Tehran is increasingly signalling that it will not accept a continuation of the status quo as the sanctions are severely impacting imports and exports to Iran. The Iranian military’s targeting of regional military facilities this week is likely related to this US economic embargo, said Andreas Krieg, an associate professor in security studies at King’s College London.

“The strikes on Bahrain and Kuwait are about probing American red lines, testing how far Tehran can push the boundaries of military confrontation without triggering another full-scale war,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.

“By targeting American assets in Gulf states, Iran is trying to make Washington’s economic warfare increasingly costly for its regional partners.”

The US military’s Central Command says its maritime blockade has prevented Iran from loading any crude oil onto its tankers since late August. It has also claimed more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude have been shipped through the Strait of Hormuz by Iran’s Arab neighbours under US protection and in defiance of demands for vessels to use a route Tehran has authorised.

Iran continues to sell oil stored outside the blockade limits to China, although at reduced levels.

The IRGC maintains that the strait remains closed to unauthorised transit and continues to target the oil shuttle system, which it believes is run primarily by the United Arab Emirates. This relay system has succeeded in getting more energy exports out of the Gulf using tankers that transfer their cargoes to other ships that deliver the oil to global markets.

The UAE’s state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) confirmed on Wednesday that one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and one crew member was missing.

To reopen the strategic waterway, Tehran has demanded the US lift its blockade and an Iran-Oman deal outlining coordinated transit routes in the strait be honoured along with other carefully sequenced US concessions on lifting the sanctions on Iran and releasing its frozen assets.

Mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to try to bridge the gaps between the two sides, but the talks have largely reached an impasse as both sides refuse to budge on their main demands.

Eslami said Trump and his senior political and military officials have failed to adopt a clear strategy towards Tehran, particularly in light of Iran’s promise of a response across the region and beyond if attacked.

“The “Iron Gate” and other measures are effectively a pretty name for their indecision,” he said about the US plan to create overland trade disruptions. “The issue in the negotiations is that they don’t know what to do about the raised proposals due to the political costs they would have to pay in the US.”

‘Pushing thresholds’

Still, some Iranians appear to believe they are the dominant party in the current impasse. Speaking to state television on Wednesday, the IRGC’s political deput,y Yadollah Javani, said Trump was stuck in a “quagmire” and must accept defeat.

“Trump has no choice but to accept realities in the field,” he said, adding that Iran was upgrading its arsenal and prepared for another major outbreak in fighting with the US.

After a third US aircraft carrier strike group entered the Arabian Sea, Iran’s army chief, Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were prepared for any new attacks by Washington.

“The enemy is preparing its forces, but the army and other armed forces monitor their movements vigilantly,” he said in a speech on Wednesday. “The preparedness of armed forces increases by the moment. Our response to any error by the enemy and its backers will be more decisive than before.”

Trump’s administration appears split on how to handle Iran with hawks such as Defense Secretary Pete Hesgeth reportedly wanting a more forceful approach to Tehran.

Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said others believe Washington can maintain the blockade and economic pressure indefinitely while avoiding full-scale war. But the latest attacks demonstrate the difficulty of maintaining such an arrangement.

“Beyond the risk of unintended escalation, the longer the blockade and economic pressure campaigns continue, the greater the incentive for Tehran to deliberately escalate in an attempt to break the deadlock by force,” he wrote in an analysis online.

Krieg said he expects Tehran to intensify calibrated pressure through attacks on US military assets and by continuing to target vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

This strategy could also potentially press the Iran-allied Houthis, the Yemeni armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), to make further advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait, another strategic chokepoint for maritime trade and global energy supplies.

“But this equilibrium is inherently unstable. If diplomacy fails to produce tangible economic relief, I believe further escalation will become increasingly likely,” Krieg said. “The greatest danger is that both sides keep pushing each other’s thresholds until one crosses a red line neither fully understood.”

entries.title: ‘Crimea is turning into an island’: How Ukraine hit Putin’s prized bridge
entries.summary: A weeks-long operation was behind two waves of strikes using long-range missiles and drones developed in Ukraine.
entries.content:
A weeks-long operation was behind two waves of strikes using long-range missiles and drones developed in Ukraine.

It was a symbolic blow for Moscow and a sign of Kyiv’s growing tactical and technological prowess.

The Ukrainian military had worked for weeks to knock out Russian air defence systems, radars and drone jamming equipment guarding the only bridge that links southern Russia to Crimea.

On Tuesday, it launched two precision attacks on the crossing with heavy drones and cruise missiles. One of the bridge’s arches collapsed, blocking the movement of cars and limiting the movement of trains to one track, while about 200 metres (660 feet) of the tarmac was heavily damaged and submerged.

“Logistically speaking, Crimea is turning into an island,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.

According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, drones developed by Kyiv hit the bridge at night, while Ukrainian Neptune missiles were among the weapons that targeted the rail section. Ukrainian-made Flamingo missiles were also involved in the operation, he said.

Netherlands-based company Destinus told the Reuters news agency that seven of its Ruta cruise missiles hit the bridge during the multistage operation.

The arch fell into the deepest part of the Kerch Strait, preventing the passage of freighters coming from southwestern Russia or occupied Ukrainian regions from transporting grain and steel.

The blockade will further deprive Russian farmers of the ability to ship their grain to the Black Sea and beyond, including the Mediterranean – and could lead to an increase in global grain prices.

But many in Ukraine are adamant that the Kremlin is deaf to the woes of Russian farmers and businessmen.

Russian President Vladimir Putin “doesn’t care about their pockets”, Taras, a drone pilot in eastern Ukraine, told Al Jazeera. “No matter how much their economy is destroyed, he knows they’ll keep mum and suffer through.”

“Putin’s biggest problem is that he still can’t fathom how technologically advanced we have become,” Taras said, withholding his last name in accordance with wartime protocol.

Zelenskyy called the sting “unprecedented” and its execution “flawless”.

The Kremlin accused the “neo-Nazi junta” in Kyiv of escalating the war.

“The Kyiv regime keeps striking civilian targets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday.

“There is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” he said the next day, adding that Moscow is determined to “continue the hostilities”.

Putin’s prized bridge

The Crimean bridge embodies the crowning achievement of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s leadership – the Black Sea peninsula’s “return” to Russia in 2014.

The 19km (12 mile) double-arched lacework of steel and concrete cost $3.8bn and opened in 2018, four years after Crimea’s annexation.

The bridge links Crimea to Russia by straddling the Kerch Strait that divides the Sea of Azov from the Black Sea. Kyiv has long denounced its construction as “illegal”.

Each arch is 227 metres (745 feet) long and weighs thousands of tonnes. They were assembled, welded and painted with anti-corrosion coating onshore, before crews operating giant, floating construction cranes installed them on top of the bridge.

Only the Syvash, a labyrinth of lagoons, salt marshes and wetlands known as the Rotten Sea, divides Crimea from southern Ukraine. Just three strips of land were wide and firm enough for the roads and rail link that has become a symbol of Russia’s hold over Crimea.

The bridge also served as a major transport hub for millions of tourists and tens of thousands of Russian troops who invaded southern Ukraine in 2022.

The attack coincided with Putin’s trip to Shenzhen in southern China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where he is due to hold a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and United States President Donald Trump.

The destruction of the arch has gone unreported in Russian media, which described the damage as “insignificant”, causing “temporarily delayed trains”.

While many Ukrainians have celebrated the operation and posted viral memes of the attack, foreign observers offer a more sober analysis.

“There’s been practically no movement [of military personnel or supplies along the bridge] for a year, only occasional gas trucks in columns,” Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher at Germany’s Bremen University, told Al Jazeera.

He said Zelenskyy should have commissioned more mid-range drones to block roads in occupied Ukrainian regions along the Sea of Azov, where Russian supply trucks still move at “relatively low risk”. Instead, Mitrokhin explained, resources were focused on the Kerch Bridge because Zelenskyy was fixated on destroying it.

“In the military sense, the [attack] was counterproductive,” he said.

Russia strikes back

Russia has been attacking bridges in Ukraine, with equally devastating results.

On Tuesday, Russian drones and missiles damaged two of the five bridges across the Dnipro River that divides the Ukrainian capital.

Previous attacks on the crossings paralysed road and subway traffic, and Kyiv residents now spend hours in huge traffic jams.

Bridges in four more Ukrainian regions have also been damaged or destroyed in recent Russian strikes.

The attacks are part of Moscow’s new strategy to destroy the pillars of the Ukrainian economy, according to Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kushch.

“While in the past, mostly the sites of infrastructure, logistics [and] energy generation were on the strike list, these days the list of targets has extended to include hypermarket chains, mining companies, processing plants and many more sites,” he told Al Jazeera.

The aim of the military campaign is to create an “empty economic space” that would decimate Ukraine’s gross domestic product (GDP), the number of jobs and the amount of tax revenue, he said.

entries.title: Can the US and Iran sustain a ‘frozen war’?
entries.summary: Tehran may eventually decide that 'escalating confrontation' is preferable to status quo, says analyst Hamidreza Azizi.
entries.content:
Tehran may eventually decide that ‘escalating confrontation’ is preferable to the status quo, says analyst Hamidreza Azizi.

For months, Iran and the United States have been weighing a return to outright war over persevering towards a negotiated peace. But they appear to have settled on something in between.

While largely stopping short of full-blown military confrontation since July, when a June Memorandum of Understanding between the two sides fell apart, the two countries have instead intermittently traded attacks while using what economic levers they have to inflict as much pain as possible on the other side. Both have maintained blockades in and around the Strait of Hormuz, once the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies.

In recent days, Iran says it has targeted US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the US has carried out an air strike on Iran’s Qeshm island on Tuesday.

Iran has, meanwhile, continued to target ships it says have not followed its rules for passing through the critical Hormuz strait, as the US stands firm on its economic sanctions and naval blockade of Iran’s ports.

The result, if not precisely a frozen conflict, is certainly demonstrating a pattern of limited confrontation that could carry on for months without escalating into all-out war, analysts say. But sustaining this status quo would mean absorbing mounting economic and political costs that could eventually prove untenable for either side, but especially for Iran, they say.

“The two sides have very different calculations about the costs of prolonging the confrontation,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “As economic pressure mounts, Iran may become increasingly willing to take military risks to break the deadlock.”

Iran rejects ‘no war, no peace’ limbo

US President Donald Trump’s administration has appeared to shift gears on Iran following the ruling Republicans’ crushing defeat by the opposition Democratic Party in this month’s midterm elections, which both Trump and his Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged the deeply unpopular Iran war was partly to blame for.

Last week, Trump said the war was “effectively over” militarily, though he also warned that he “would not hesitate” to resume strikes if diplomacy failed.

Meanwhile, Trump’s Secretary of State Marco Rubio has suggested the US is pursuing economic pressure rather than military pressure.

“We don’t need to conduct military strikes if we’re achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure,” Rubio said last week. “The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse.”

But this plan to maintain an uneasy standoff with Iran while avoiding a return to full-blown war may not sit well in Tehran, where Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has told officials to end the state of “neither war nor peace”.

“We will not remain in a state of ‘neither war nor peace,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, told parliament on Sunday. “It makes absolutely no difference to us whether the United States wants negotiations or war.”’

‘Oil price floor’

The economic pain of a frozen conflict would be extensive for Iran, the Gulf and the global economy, analysts say.

Iran’s disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have already triggered some of the most dramatic fluctuations in the oil price in years.

In late October, Brent crude, the world’s crude oil benchmark, was trading at $117 per barrel, its highest price since April when it reached a four-year high. The price, which was about $72 just before the war began, has since fallen back to $92 per barrel as vessels brave the Strait of Hormuz, despite an uptick in attacks. But that is still 30 percent higher than before the war.

Petrol and diesel prices in the US have trended similarly. The current average for petrol is $3.80 per gallon (3.8 litres), the lowest since March, but that is still a far cry from the pre-war average of $2.98, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

The average price for diesel stands at just over $5.93 per gallon as of November 17, 2026, according to the US Energy Information Administration. That compares with $3.72 in February before the war began, and has taken a particular toll on farmers and truckers in the US – many of whom form the backbone of Trump’s MAGA support base.

Ron Bousso, a columnist who analyses global energy markets for Reuters, said he estimates that a drawn-out, low-grade conflict between the US and Iran could “put a floor under oil prices” and force Gulf oil exporters to keep contending with massive freight and insurance costs.

The danger, he wrote for Reuters last week, “⁠is not simply another dramatic surge in oil prices caused by renewed war. It is that the Middle East settles into something more durable and more insidious: a conflict intense enough to keep shipping dangerous, insurance expensive and energy infrastructure vulnerable, but contained enough for the world to learn to live with it.”

Such a scenario would mean longer-term economic strain on many of the US’s Gulf allies, while, according to Bousso, global energy disruption becomes the “new normal”.

‘Iran’s population is suffering’

The economic toll on Iran could be even more severe, however.

Week after week, the US has introduced more sanctions against not only Iranian entities, but entities it says are trading with or connected to Iran, further isolating the country from the outside world. Meanwhile, the US naval blockade has made it increasingly difficult for Iran to export its oil.

As a result, Iran’s government has continuously prioritised “short-term survival” over much-needed sustainable investment at a time when its economy is shrinking and its people are dealing with one of the world’s highest inflation rates, Mohammad Farzanegan, professor of Middle East economics at the interdisciplinary Center for Near and Middle Eastern Studies, told Al Jazeera.

Iran’s falling oil revenues, he said, “have introduced significant pressure on the government budget, increasing the need to raise taxes, reduce subsidies, especially on energy products, and plan painful economic reforms”.

“All these developments have amplified the feeling of deprivation among the population, especially the youth,” Farzanegan added.

Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, agreed that “Iran’s population is suffering tremendously”, saying “they bear the brunt of this economic war”.

“While this is not sustainable, long term the question is, if it can hold until Trump leaves office,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.

‘Fragile conditions’

The economic pressure on Iran also risks triggering political upheaval, according to Azizi and Farzanegan.

“The [Iranian] leadership is particularly concerned about the possibility of renewed domestic unrest at a time when it is confronting the United States externally,” said Azizi. “Allowing the current situation to continue indefinitely could gradually weaken the economy, increase domestic instability and undermine the government’s position.”

Farzanegan said that any new major shock, such as a natural or human-made disaster, “could ignite a new round of violent protests”.

How long Iran can maintain the status quo hinges on the extent to which it can find ways to bypass the blockade, secure alternative trade partners and tame corruption and domestic economic grievances, he said. “It is unclear how long the government can maintain stability inside Iran under such fragile economic conditions,” he added.

Will the US or Iran deliberately escalate?

There are political costs to a drawn-out conflict for the US, too.

For one, it goes against one of Trump’s core campaign pledges – no new foreign wars. Maintaining the status quo keeps alive a conflict that more than 70 percent of Americans say they want to end, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll on November 9.

“There is also the question of credibility,” said Azizi. “The United States has demonstrated its overwhelming military superiority, but it has so far been unable to compel Iran to abandon its control over the strait or accept Washington’s terms. The longer this situation continues, the more difficult it becomes to explain what the American strategy is ultimately supposed to achieve.”

As a result, analysts say, there are reasons that both Iran and the US could choose to escalate, triggering a return to war.

Iran’s government, said Azizi, “may eventually conclude that deliberately escalating the confrontation is preferable to allowing its economic and strategic position to deteriorate further”.

Trump’s blistering midterm election defeat, on the other hand, has “removed the last consideration we all thought would hold him back from a full-scale war”, said Parsi.

Trump still has the option of letting sanctions run their course, he added, but if he comes to believe that another military attack “will spell the end of the Islamic republic, or simply wants revenge, this ‘not-peace’ could easily become a full war”.

entries.title: What’s holding South Africa’s economy back?
entries.summary: South Africa seeks billions in new investment to revive weak growth and tackle unemployment crisis.
entries.content:
Counting the Cost

What’s holding South Africa’s economy back?

South Africa seeks billions in new investment to revive weak growth and tackle unemployment crisis.

Africa’s most industrialised economy faces an unemployment crisis.

And last year, more foreign investment left South Africa than came in.

Years of power shortages, crumbling infrastructure and corruption have shaken confidence.

One estimate says South Africa needs an additional $75bn a year to revive growth.

President Cyril Ramaphosa is courting US tech giants to help make South Africa an AI hub.

But Washington has hit South Africa with steep tariffs and is cutting its duty-free access to the US market.

Pretoria is increasingly looking to China.

So, can South Africa win back investors and turn promises into jobs?

Published On 18 Nov 2026

Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah is set to face a retrial before an Egyptian criminal court on Wednesday, after being sentenced in absentia to one year in prison for operating an unlicensed website and spreading ‘false news’. The court has also ordered the closure of the independent news outlet.

entries.title: What is the ‘endgame’ in Syria, as Israeli rivals look for new government?
entries.summary: As Israel intensifies its incursions into southern Syria, analysts say there will be little change in the future.
entries.content:
As Israel intensifies its incursions into southern Syria, analysts say there will be little change in the future.

As Israel’s post-election political scenario continues to unfold, analysts and experts tell Al Jazeera that Israel’s occupation of parts of southern Syria is likely to continue regardless of who becomes the country’s next prime minister.

Israeli incursions and raids in the provinces of Quneitra and Deraa intensified in recent weeks as Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and de facto leader of the opposition Gadi Eisenkot try to form a new government.

Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Israel has occupied key strategic points in southern Syria, such as Jabal al-Sheikh, which Israelis know as Mount Hermon.

Israel’s continued violations of Syrian sovereignty are piling pressure on the new government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus, which has been targeted in Israeli air strikes. Syria has sought to harness its deepening ties with regional and international powers to pressure Israel to stop its incursions, but this strategy does not yet appear to be bearing fruit.

Israeli raids, often resulting in detentions or civilian deaths, are leading to continued instability in southern Syria, which has already suffered from the 14-year war between al-Assad’s forces and the opposition. But even with a prospective change in government in Israel following last month’s election, the endgame has not changed for Israel, analysts say.

“Israel appears to want both to dematerialise the south and the freedom to intervene there,” Navvar Saban, a researcher in security and military affairs at the Arab Center for Contemporary Syrian Studies in Damascus, told Al Jazeera.

“Israel is turning its military presence into an established reality before any settlement. Repeated incursions, checkpoints, construction, [are all] strengthening its control and negotiation leverage.”

Military raids

Syrians in areas close to the Israeli occupation of their land live in a constant state of fear, with homes being raided and civilians being arrested. The fate of 35 Syrians detained by Israel is still unknown, according to a report by the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR).

Israeli forces have also conducted a series of air and artillery strikes on villages and countryside in southern Syria, with 69 people killed since 2024, the SNHR report said.

On Tuesday, a video emerged of an Israeli raid in the province of Deraa, one of the areas heavily targeted by Israel.

Israeli forces left a local home with bullet holes in the window, walls charred with soot, and belongings tossed across the floor. Locals and experts say Israeli troops routinely raid homes and detain residents in the area, while Syrian authorities appear powerless to prevent them.

Syria’s biggest challenge

Israel has occupied the Golan Heights since 1967 and illegally annexed the strategic Syrian territory in 1981. In December 2024, during the collapse of the al-Assad regime, Israel invaded and occupied neutral areas of the Golan, along with more Syrian lands. Over the next year, Syria was attacked more than 600 times, despite the new government in Damascus saying it posed no threat to Israel.

For the past two years, Syria’s stated priorities have mostly been internal. The new government has worked to remove international sanctions and spur a stuttering local economy. Internationally, Syria has said it wants no problems with its neighbours and has tried to reintegrate the country into the regional fold after years of broken relations under al-Assad.

But since October 2023, when the genocide in Gaza began, Israel has adopted a more outwardly aggressive strategy with its neighbours, including Lebanon and Syria. In recent months, Israel has been intensifying its incursions and raids on southern Syria in particular.

A report published in late October by the Arab Reform Initiative found that Israel had conducted 678 ground incursions and 168 raids into southern Syria between January and September 2026. In September alone, it launched 113 incursions, 27 raids and 24 artillery shelling incidents into southern Syria, showing what the report called “a trend toward escalation”.

Due to the situation, government officials have been prevented from performing their duties in many parts of southern Syria, effectively putting these areas under Israeli security control. Syrians arrested by Israeli forces have recounted brutal prison conditions, including physical and psychological abuse.

Externally, this is the biggest “challenge for al-Sharaa and his government” Issam al-Reis, a senior military adviser and research director at Damascus-based nonprofit Etana Syria, told Al Jazeera.

“Everything else could be solved, including Suwayda and the integration of the SDF, but the truth is this is the biggest concern to the government,” he said, referring to the Syrian Democratic Forces, officially dissolved in August.

New government, little change

Israeli elections last month came with the prospect of a new government.

Matan Kahana was elected parliament speaker on Tuesday, in a blow to the prospect of Netanyahu returning to power. He is an ally of Eisenkot, the Yashar party leader invited to form the next government to replace Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.

But analysts say even if Eisenkot succeeds and forms a government, there will be few changes in Israel’s policy on Syria.

“The [Israeli] government could change their diplomatic approach, but I would not assume it would abandon Israel’s security demands or withdraw automatically,” researcher Saban said. “The security demands for the Israelis will never change. The ratio of it might change, the approach might change. But the security demand is always present in the Israeli mentality.”

Al-Reis, who is also a former military officer who defected from the Syrian Army, said decisions taken by Israel in southern Syria are dictated by military matters and not political concerns.

“Therefore, it will not change as a result of the electoral government change,” he said.

Even Israeli soldiers who have taken part in the occupation of southern Syria have said they are unconvinced by the army and the government’s narrative that southern Syria poses a security concern to Israel.

“The feeling [is] that there’s some bluff everybody is playing along with. We’re there, so we need to invent a story that it’s dangerous,” one soldier told the Israeli daily Haaretz.

Without a clear policy or mission, troops fire at civilians, shoot at animals, or conduct night-time searches during which families are pulled from their beds, detained and questioned, similar to Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank.

Arrests, disappearances

Israel has claimed it is in southern Syria to counter groups opposed to Iran operating in the territory, although since the fall of the al-Assad government, Iran-linked militias have been withdrawn.

Still, since then it has at various times alleged that the ISIL (ISIS) group and Lebanon’s branch of the Muslim Brotherhood are present in Syria, although the latter denies it operates outside Lebanon’s borders.

Saban said, because many residents of southern Deraa and Quneitra are farmers, guns are present in the region, but this is far from the narrative painted by the Israeli military.

“It’s a weaponised culture [because] they are farmers with herds, but resistance to incursion is not automatically evidence of an organised, externally directed network,” he said. “The Israelis are trying to project that the whole area is an organised resistance. But there isn’t any organised resistance. People having arms over there does not mean that they are part of a network.”

Saban believes that Israel’s presence and endgame in southern Syria are less about beating back the so-called resistance and more about creating a new reality on the ground. This is one in which the Israeli military can operate freely without opposition from locals or the Syrian government.

“It is clear that there is no intention at all to withdraw from Syrian territory,” al-Reis said.

entries.title: How the US House of Representatives chooses its leaders: A visual guide
entries.summary: After their midterm win, Democrats will lead the House from January 3. Here’s how its speaker and leaders are chosen.
entries.content:
After their midterm win, Democrats will lead the House from January 3. Here’s how its speaker and leaders are chosen.

House Democrats will vote on Wednesday to choose their leaders for the new Congress, with Hakeem Jeffries expected to win the party’s nomination for speaker. He faces no declared challenger.

If he wins the full House vote on January 3, the New York Democrat, who succeeded Nancy Pelosi as his party’s House leader in 2023, would become the first Black speaker in United States history.

His path is clear after Democrats won control of the House in the November 3 midterm elections, ending two years of Republican control under President Donald Trump. As of Wednesday, Democrats have won 257 of the House’s 435 seats and Republicans have won 171, with seven races still to be called, according to The Associated Press news agency.

In this visual guide, Al Jazeera explains the roles of the speaker, majority and minority leaders and whips, how the speaker is elected, and what happens on January 3, when power changes hands.

Who runs the House of Representatives?

The House of Representatives, the lower chamber of Congress, has 435 members elected every two years. It passes laws with the Senate and controls government spending.

Each party chooses its own leaders. As the new majority, Democrats will hold the speaker’s chair and the majority posts, and Republicans will take the minority roles. The main jobs are:

  • Speaker: runs the House and decides which bills get a vote. Second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president.
  • Majority leader: sets the House agenda and steers the majority party’s bills.
  • Minority leader: leads the opposition party in the House.
  • Whips: count votes and keep each party’s members in line.

On November 10, Republicans chose Jim Jordan of Ohio as minority leader and Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip. The outgoing speaker, Mike Johnson, did not run.

On Wednesday, Democrats will also vote on the rest of their leadership team. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is running for majority leader, which would make her the first woman to hold the post, and Pete Aguilar of California is running for majority whip.

Senate Democrats face a contested race. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Chuck Schumer, the party’s leader in the Senate since 2017, in a vote in early December.

How is a speaker chosen?

Choosing a speaker takes two votes.

First, each party picks its candidate in a secret ballot behind closed doors. Winning that vote makes a candidate the party’s nominee, not yet the speaker.

Then, on January 3, the full House votes, with each member saying aloud the name of their preferred candidate.

To win, a candidate needs a majority of the votes cast for a named person, which is 218 if all 435 members vote. Members who vote “present” or are absent lower that number.

If no one reaches a majority, the House votes again until someone does. Until then, it cannot swear in members or pass laws.

Most speakers win on the first ballot, but not all. In January 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy needed 15 ballots over four days to win the job, the first time in a century that a speaker election had gone to a second ballot.

In October 2023, McCarthy also became the first speaker removed by a House vote, leaving the chamber without a speaker for three weeks.

With a large majority behind him, Jeffries is unlikely to face such a fight. Some progressives, particularly newly elected members, have withheld their support, seeking commitments on halting US military aid to Israel and on campaign finance reform. But no one has stepped forward to run against him. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, whose petition on the party’s agenda sparked talk of a challenge, said on Monday she would not run.

Jeffries has called for a recorded vote rather than approval by acclamation, a move that will put any opposition within his party on record.

What happens on January 3?

At noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, the old Congress ends and the new one begins.

In the House chamber, in the south wing of the US Capitol, the speaker vote comes first. Once the winner is sworn in, the new speaker swears in every member at once. The House then sets its rules for the next two years, and each party’s leaders take up their posts.

In the Senate chamber, in the Capitol’s north wing, Vice President JD Vance swears in the newly elected senators. The Senate also chooses a president pro tempore, usually the majority’s most senior senator, to preside in the vice president’s absence.

The handover begins a period of divided government: a Republican president and a Democratic Congress.

Democrats will be able to block Trump’s agenda and investigate his administration. Trump can veto their bills, and overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

The date is set by the Constitution, though Congress can change it by law. In 2027, January 3 falls on a Sunday.
